Respiratory System

The organs that bring air in and out, and the tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the blood.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Name the organs of the respiratory tract in the correct order
  • Describe the lungs, pleura and diaphragm
  • Explain where and how gas exchange happens

In simple words

Breathing is not the same as respiration. Breathing (ventilation) moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is the whole process: taking in oxygen, using it in cells, and removing carbon dioxide.

Air travels along one road:

Nose → Pharynx → Larynx → Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Alveoli

The lungs do not have muscles of their own. They expand because the diaphragm and intercostal muscles pull the chest open, and air rushes in.

The organs, one by one

Part What it does
Nose Warms, moistens and filters air; detects smell
Pharynx Common passage for air and food (the “throat”)
Larynx Voice box; guards the airway during swallowing
Trachea Windpipe; C-shaped cartilage rings keep it open
Bronchi Right and left main branches entering each lung
Bronchioles Smaller branches with smooth muscle; can narrow in asthma
Alveoli Tiny air sacs; the only place where gas exchange happens
Pleura Double membrane around the lung; fluid between layers reduces friction

🔴 The one line that wins marks

Gas exchange happens only in the alveoli. Everything before it is just a pipeline.

How breathing works

  1. The diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the ribs move up and out.
  2. The chest cavity gets bigger, so pressure inside falls.
  3. Air rushes in (inspiration). This is active.
  4. The diaphragm relaxes, the chest gets smaller, and air flows out (expiration). This is passive at rest.

Gas exchange in the alveolus

Oxygen (blue) moves from the alveolus into the blood. Carbon dioxide (grey) moves from blood into the alveolus to be breathed out.

Numbers you must remember

Measurement Normal adult value
Respiratory rate 12–20 breaths per minute
Tidal volume (air per normal breath) about 500 mL
Vital capacity about 4,500–5,000 mL
Oxygen in room air 21%
Oxygen carried by haemoglobin about 97% saturation
Carbon dioxide carried as bicarbonate about 70%

Where the nurse uses this

  • Positioning: sitting upright (Fowler’s) lets the diaphragm move down and improves breathing.
  • Oxygen therapy: humidify oxygen, check the prescription, watch for dryness of the nose.
  • Suctioning: clear secretions from the mouth, nose or trachea when the patient cannot cough.
  • Chest physiotherapy: percussion, vibration and postural drainage move mucus toward the larger airways.
  • Incentive spirometer: encourages deep breathing after surgery to prevent collapse of alveoli (atelectasis).

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Correct order: nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
  2. Right lung has 3 lobes, left lung has 2 lobes (space for the heart).
  3. Alveoli are the site of gas exchange; their thin walls and rich capillaries make this possible.
  4. Diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration; expiration at rest is passive.
  5. Two pleura: parietal (attached to chest wall) and visceral (on the lung), with pleural fluid between them.
  6. Normal adult respiratory rate is 12–20 per minute.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Trachea is kept open by C-shaped cartilage rings; the gap at the back allows the food pipe to expand.
  2. Bronchioles have smooth muscle and no cartilage — hence they narrow in asthma.
  3. Tidal volume is about 500 mL; vital capacity is about 4,500–5,000 mL.
  4. The nose warms, moistens and filters air before it reaches the lungs.

📌 Memory trick

Order of the airway: “Nurses Please Listen To Breathing Better Always” — Nose, Pharynx, Larynx, Trachea, Bronchi, Bronchioles, Alveoli.

60-second revision

  • Air path: nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
  • Right lung 3 lobes; left lung 2 lobes.
  • Alveoli = gas exchange. O₂ in, CO₂ out.
  • Diaphragm contracts → air in. Relaxes → air out.
  • Pleura = two layers with fluid; reduces friction.
  • Normal adult respiratory rate 12–20/min.

Test yourself

Which structure is the actual site of gas exchange?

Answer: C. Alveoli have thin walls and a dense capillary network, so oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse across.

How many lobes are present in the right lung?

Answer: C. The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, lower). The left has two, because the heart takes up space.

The main muscle of inspiration is the:

Answer: A. The diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity and pulling air in.

Which cartilage keeps the trachea from collapsing?

Answer: A. The trachea has C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings. The gap at the back lets the oesophagus expand during swallowing.

A normal respiratory rate for a healthy adult is:

Answer: B. 12–20 breaths per minute is normal for adults at rest. Rates are higher in children.

⭐ Exam answer tip

For a 5-mark question, draw the air-path diagram, name the organs in order, and write two lines on the alveoli. That structure alone usually earns full marks.
